user_message:
A regional water utility has established a utilities dynamic market for routine maintenance works and has already published a qualifying dynamic market notice to advertise it. The utility now wants to award a specific maintenance contract to suppliers who are already members of that market rather than running a fresh open competition. The procurement officer is unsure whether the usual public tender notice route still has to be followed, or whether a different notification process applies because the suppliers are already inside an established market.

We've set up a utilities dynamic market for our maintenance work and want to award a contract to companies already inside it. Do we still need to publish a normal public tender notice for this award, or does a different process apply to notifying the market members?

A district council's commercial team is planning a facilities management contract with an estimated whole-life value of around £195,000, excluding VAT. The council is a sub-central (i.e. not central government) contracting authority. The team needs to establish whether this value brings the contract within the full procurement regime as a regulated public contract, or whether it falls under the below-threshold rules instead, since that determines which set of publication duties apply from the outset.

We're about to run a facilities management procurement worth around £195,000 for the council. How do we work out whether this contract has to go through the full procurement process, or whether it counts as below the relevant threshold for a body like ours?

A central government department has completed a competitive tendering procedure for a services contract and has decided on a winning bidder. The contract manager wants to sign the contract as quickly as possible, but a losing bidder has already hinted it may challenge the outcome. The contract manager needs to know exactly how long the department must wait after notifying the market of the award decision before the contract can actually be signed.

We've decided who's won our tender and want to sign the contract quickly, but a losing bidder is unhappy. How long do we legally have to wait after telling the market about the award decision before we can actually sign the contract?

An NHS trust is evaluating a bidder for a facilities contract. The trust's own records show that this supplier significantly underperformed on a previous contract with a different NHS body, was given a proper opportunity to improve, and still failed to meet the required standard. Legal advice is being sought both on whether the trust can act on this history in the current competition and on whether the matter could be escalated so that the supplier is considered for a government-wide debarment listing.

One of our bidders has a documented history of failing to meet contract standards for another NHS body, even after being given a chance to improve. Can we take that into account when deciding whether this supplier can compete for our contract, and separately, is there a route for that kind of track record to lead to the supplier being barred from public contracts more broadly?

A central government department's commercial policy team wants to alert the market to a major upcoming IT procurement several months before the formal tender process begins, so that suppliers have time to prepare and mobilise resources. The team is checking whether publishing this kind of early notice is a legal requirement or a voluntary option, and what information it would need to contain if they choose to publish one.

We want to alert the market early about a big IT procurement that's still months away from going out to tender, so suppliers have time to prepare. Is publishing that kind of early notice something we're required to do, and what would we need to include in it?

A council ran a full open competition for a school catering contract. Only one tender was received, and on evaluation it materially failed the specification and would have been disregarded under the authority's own published assessment methodology. The incumbent contract expires in six weeks and there is no time to re-run the full competition.

We published a full tender competition for this contract but the only response we got doesn't meet our requirements and would fail evaluation anyway. Can we just go and agree a contract with a supplier we already trust instead of running the competition again, and is there anything we have to publish first if we do that?

An NHS trust is procuring a routine medical consumables contract under budget pressure. The finance lead wants to skip any quality or service scoring entirely and award purely to whichever compliant bidder quotes the lowest total price.

Is it actually allowed for us to score bids purely on price and ignore quality altogether, or do we always have to build in some kind of non-price scoring criteria?

A central government department is finalising a tender pack for a services contract. The legal team has asked bid teams to require that (a) bidders already have contract-specific insurance in place before the contract is signed, and (b) every bidder, including very small suppliers, submit three years of audited financial statements.

Before we finalise the tender pack, can we insist bidders already have the contract-specific insurance in place before we award, and can we require audited accounts from every single bidder, even the very small ones?

A water utility wants to set up a framework for a major capital works programme expected to run for around ten years, given the scale of infrastructure investment and the time suppliers need to recoup mobilisation costs.

Our capital programme arrangement needs to run well beyond the usual term cap on these agreements - is there a route that lets us keep something like this going for a decade, and if so what does setting it up that way actually require us to build in from the start?

A council has been running a qualified-supplier list for temporary agency staff for eighteen months. To cut administrative overhead, the category manager wants to stop assessing new supplier applications for the rest of the arrangement's life and just keep working with the suppliers already on the list.

Once we've got a solid working group of suppliers on our staffing list, can we just close it to new joiners for a while to cut down on admin, or are we required to keep taking new applications the whole time the arrangement runs?

A university is scoping a five-year estates maintenance contract worth several million pounds. It has always been let as one large single contract to one national provider, but the sustainability team has raised concerns that this locks out smaller regional and specialist contractors from ever bidding.

Before we go out to market on this one, do we actually have to stop and think about splitting it into smaller packages to give smaller firms a chance, or can we just carry on letting it as one big contract like we always have?

A government department is about to sign a seven-million-pound contract for high-level strategic policy advisory services, where outputs are largely qualitative and evolve throughout the engagement.

This contract is well above the usual reporting threshold - are we legally required to set specific measurable performance indicators for it no matter what, or is there any get-out if the kind of work just doesn't lend itself to that kind of scoring?

We are running a competition for a highways maintenance contract. One of the bidders performed very badly on a waste-collection contract for a neighbouring council two years ago, with persistent late running and defects the council had to fix itself. Nobody ever took the bidder to court over it, and there was no formal finding against them. We are trying to work out whether we are even allowed to hold that history against them at the shortlisting stage.

A bidder has a well-documented history of seriously underperforming on a previous public contract, even though nobody sued them over it or got a court ruling. Are we allowed to factor that track record into whether they can take part in our competition, and if so, what do we need to be able to show?

We're about to award a large IT services contract centrally. Before signing, one of the team asked whether there is a central register we're obliged to check to rule out bidders who have effectively been shut out of public sector work government-wide, as opposed to being excluded only from our own specific competition.

Is there a government-wide list of suppliers who are barred from all public contracts, and are we required to check it before we sign, or does exclusion only ever operate competition-by-competition?

Six months into a facilities management contract, we discovered that the contractor's parent company was convicted of a serious fraud offence shortly after we signed. Nothing like this was known to us, or discoverable, at the time of contract award. Some colleagues want to let the contract keep running since day-to-day service is fine; others think we have to act because of what's come to light.

If a supplier becomes caught up in something that would normally have kept them out of the running, but this only comes to light after the contract has already started, can we pull the plug on the deal now, and what do we have to do before and after we do?

Our estates team has a five-year grounds-maintenance contract with a single supplier. Fuel and wage costs have risen in ways nobody could reasonably have predicted when the original competition was run, and the supplier says it cannot keep delivering at the agreed price. We would rather adjust the price with the existing supplier than start a brand-new competition from scratch.

If costs on a live contract rise for reasons nobody could have seen coming, how far can we adjust the price with our existing supplier before that change becomes big enough that we would be required to go back out to competition instead?

We've identified our preferred bidder for a new energy-metering framework and want to move quickly to signature. Someone in finance mentioned there might be a mandatory pause we have to observe before we can actually commit to the contract.

Once we've picked a winning bidder, is there a mandatory waiting period we must observe before we can sign the contract, how long is it, and are there any situations where we can go straight to signature without waiting?

We ran an open competitive tendering procedure for a highways resurfacing contract. Only one tender was submitted, and it was disregarded because the supplier failed to meet a mandatory technical requirement, so in practice we received no suitable tender at all. Senior management wants to move quickly and place the contract directly with a contractor we already trust, rather than re-running the whole procedure.

Can we switch straight to a direct award with a supplier of our choosing after a competitive procedure produced no suitable tenders, and if so what do we need to check or publish before we go ahead?

An NHS trust has an existing facilities management contract. Six months into the term, an additional building has come into use earlier than planned, and the trust wants to add that building to the scope of the existing contract rather than tendering separately. The change would increase the contract's value by roughly 12 per cent.

Are we allowed to add this extra building to the existing contract without starting a fresh procurement, and is there anything we have to publish before we make the change?

A university group is setting up a new framework for IT hardware and managed services. Because of long technology refresh and integration cycles, the commercial team wants the framework to run for six years, longer than they believe is normally allowed.

Is there a hard cap on how long a new framework can run, and if we want to go beyond the usual limit because of the nature of what we're buying, is there anything specific we need to record or publish?

A government department is designing a novel digital case-management system and wants to speak informally with a small number of specialist suppliers before going out to tender, to understand what is technically feasible and refine the specification.

Are we allowed to talk to suppliers like this before we go out to tender, what do we need to do to keep it fair to everyone, and is there anything we need to publish about it?

A council's finance team has just gone live with a new invoicing system for a large multi-year highways maintenance contract, and contract managers want to understand their statutory obligations around paying the contractor's invoices.

Is there a legal deadline by which we must pay this supplier's invoices, and do we have any separate obligation to report on how well we're paying on time?

A council needs several batches of similar specialist furniture for different sites over the coming year. Each individual order would come in comfortably under the council's procurement threshold, and a colleague has suggested placing them as separate below-threshold purchases to avoid running a full tender.

Can we deliberately structure these as separate smaller purchases to stay under the threshold, and if we do have a genuinely below-threshold contract, what do we still need to publish?

A council is planning a regional grounds-maintenance procurement covering several district areas. The commercial team is deciding whether to run it as one large contract or split it geographically, and is also wary of a single contractor winning every area and becoming a point of failure.

Do we actually have to consider splitting this into separate area-based contracts, and if we do go with separate lots, can we limit how many a single bidder is allowed to win?

Corrigan Vale District Council awarded a five-year highways resurfacing and maintenance contract in January 2025 following a competitive tender run entirely under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015. The Procurement Act 2023 has since come fully into force. The council's commercial team now wants to instruct additional resurfacing works using a price-revision options clause that was included in the original tender documents, and needs to know which set of rules currently governs any change to this specific contract.

We ran our competition and awarded this contract under the old procurement regulations, just before the new Procurement Act rules came into force. We now want to use an options clause from our original tender documents to instruct some extra resurfacing works. Does a live contract like this automatically move onto the new Act's rules for making changes now that the Act is in force, or does something else determine which rulebook we follow?

A central government department wants to commission a short piece of research from a specialist consultancy at an estimated value of about £18,000, without running a full competitive tender. Some colleagues in the department have suggested that because the contract's value is well below the international-agreement procurement thresholds, none of the Procurement Act 2023's rules need to be complied with at all before the department goes ahead.

We're about to award a contract worth roughly £18,000 to a consultancy without running a full competition, since it's a small piece of work that's well below the usual procurement threshold. Before we go ahead, do we still have any publication or notice duties under the Procurement Act, or does the Act simply not apply once you're below the main threshold figure?

A university set up a four-year framework for temporary academic and administrative staffing three years ago. It was not established as part of a rolling 'open framework' scheme, and it is not a defence, security or utilities framework. With the framework due to expire soon, the university's category manager would like to simply extend it for a further two years rather than running a fresh competition, since re-tendering mid-academic-year would be disruptive.

We have a staffing framework that's coming up to its expiry date, and we'd like to just extend it for another couple of years rather than re-running the whole competition, since it's working well operationally. Is there a hard statutory limit on how long a framework like this can run, or can we extend it by agreement if both sides are willing?

An NHS trust holds a multi-supplier facilities management framework. It has just run a mini-competition among the framework suppliers and wants to place a call-off contract with the winning supplier. Contract managers at the trust are used to observing a mandatory pre-contract standstill period whenever they award contracts following a full open competition and assume the same rule must apply here.

We're about to award a call-off contract to one of our framework suppliers after running a mini-competition between them. Do we have to observe the same mandatory standstill period before we sign that we would for a contract awarded through a full open tender, or does the position differ for call-off contracts under a framework?

A local authority is midway through evaluating tenders in a live procurement. One bidder marked its pricing schedule and technical method statement as commercially confidential when it submitted its tender. Before the contract is awarded, the authority receives a Freedom of Information request from a local journalist asking for full copies of all tenders received, including pricing.

We've had an FOI request asking for full copies of the tenders in an ongoing procurement, including a bidder's pricing, which they've told us is commercially sensitive. Can we withhold that information, and what would we need to be able to show if the requester or the bidder challenged our decision?

Our authority is about to award a £6.2 million grounds maintenance and winter gritting contract to a single supplier. This is our first contract over the £5 million threshold since the new procurement regime came into force, and our contract management team has not previously had to run a formal KPI regime linked to statutory notices. We need to build the ongoing monitoring and reporting cycle into our contract management plan before the contract starts.

We're about to enter into a £6.2 million grounds maintenance contract. What should our ongoing key performance indicator process look like once the contract is live -- how many KPIs do we need, and how often do we need to assess and publish performance against them?

A central government department runs several multi-year facilities and IT support contracts, each with layers of sub-contractors. Following recent changes to the procurement rules, the finance and commercial teams have been asked to jointly design a payment monitoring process that will let the department demonstrate compliance without waiting for an external audit to flag problems. No such process currently exists across the department's contract portfolio.

We want to set up an internal process for monitoring and reporting on payment performance across our contracts and their supply chains. What information do we need to track, and how often do we need to publish it, to stay compliant?

An NHS trust is planning to replace its diagnostic imaging service ahead of a major tender, and wants to talk to manufacturers and service providers early to understand what solutions are realistically available before finalising its specification. The category manager is conscious that the trust has an existing supplier for related equipment and does not want the process to be seen as tailoring the eventual competition around that supplier.

We want to talk to potential suppliers before we go out to tender, to understand what's available and help us write a realistic specification, but we're worried this could be seen as favouring our existing supplier or distorting the eventual competition. What do we actually need to do to run this safely?

A university is preparing to re-tender its combined grounds maintenance and cleaning services across several campuses in different towns. Historically this has been awarded as one large contract to a single national provider, but the estates team wants to know whether the rules now require them to think about dividing the requirement into separate lots, and what they need to do if they decide to keep it as one contract.

Before we go out to tender for our combined estates services contract across several campuses, do we need to consider splitting the requirement into lots, and what do we need to record if we decide to keep it as a single contract?

A council frequently procures small, similar-value repairs and minor works packages throughout the year and wants to stop running a full tender exercise each time. It is considering establishing a standing pool of qualified suppliers it can call off from as work arises, and wants to understand practically how such a pool is set up and kept compliant, including what happens if a supplier on the list later becomes subject to an exclusion ground.

We're considering setting up a rolling pool of pre-qualified suppliers for repeat minor works, rather than re-tendering every time. What's the practical process for establishing this and keeping the supplier list compliant over time, including what we need to do if a supplier on the list later becomes an excluded supplier?

A central government department's commercial team has just been told by the Cabinet Office that one of its suppliers has been entered onto the published debarment list following an investigation. The supplier has written to the department stating that it intends to challenge the decision, and a commercial colleague has already told the department's legal adviser (based on a law firm blog post) that the supplier can simply ask the Minister informally to reconsider. Before replying to the supplier's letter, the legal adviser wants to check what the actual legal mechanism for challenging a debarment listing is, including any time limits and what a court can and cannot do.

Is there an actual statutory route for a supplier to challenge being placed on the debarment list, with a defined time limit and remedy, or is that just something people describe informally? I need the real legal mechanism here, not a summary from a blog.

A local authority's commercial manager has received a Freedom of Information request from a local journalist asking for the full pricing breakdown submitted by the winning bidder in a recently awarded contract. The winning supplier has objected, saying the figures were marked confidential in its tender and should not be released. A colleague has told the commercial manager that marking something 'confidential' in a tender automatically means it can be withheld, but the commercial manager is not convinced that is actually how the law works.

We've had an FOI request for a supplier's pricing information from a contract we just awarded, and the supplier says it's commercially sensitive. Is there an actual legal exemption that lets us withhold it, and what's the real test that applies, not just what the supplier assumes because they marked it confidential?

A procurement officer at a university is running a multi-stage competitive procedure and is about to let bidders progress to the next stage. A colleague mentioned that checking whether a bidder has a history of past misconduct that could affect its standing is 'best practice' but not something the university is legally obliged to do unless the bidder already appears on the published debarment list. The procurement officer wants to check whether that is actually correct before letting anyone through to the next stage.

Before we let a bidder move on to the next stage of our procurement, is there an actual legal requirement to check whether they should be excluded, or is that just recommended good practice? I want to know what the law itself requires, not a training summary.

A county council's highways team invited tenders for a term maintenance contract through an open competitive tendering procedure. All of the tenders received were rejected as technically non-compliant with the specification, and no compliant bids remain in play. The team is under time pressure to get a contractor mobilised before winter gritting season and is considering placing the contract directly with one of the bidders that submitted a rejected tender, rather than re-running the competition. Nobody on the team has pinned down exactly when, in procurement-process terms, the original tendering exercise is treated as having started, which matters given the recent change in the procurement rules.

We invited tenders for a highways contract but every bid we got back was rejected as unsuitable. Can we now just award the contract directly to one of those bidders without starting a new competition, and what do we need to check or publish before doing that?

An NHS trust's commercial team put in place a multi-supplier framework for clinical equipment maintenance a few years ago. One of the suppliers on the framework has asked for an 18-month extension to its individual call-off contract because of ongoing supply-chain disruption affecting spare parts. Separately, the trust is approaching the point where it would otherwise need to re-run the framework competition, and someone has suggested simply rolling the existing framework forward instead of starting a fresh procurement. Nobody has flagged whether the framework was set up before or after the most recent change in procurement legislation.

One of our framework suppliers wants an 18-month extension on their call-off contract because of supply problems, and separately we're wondering whether we can just extend the framework itself rather than re-competing it when it reaches its original end date. Are either of those changes allowed without a new procurement, and how far could we realistically go?

A central government department has a services contract where the supplier has repeatedly missed the performance targets set out at the start of the contract, despite being told about it and given time to put things right. The department's contract manager wants to terminate but isn't sure whether repeated poor performance against the targets is, by itself, a lawful ground for termination, or whether anything needs to be formally reported or published about the poor performance regardless of what is decided about the contract itself. The contract's own termination clauses haven't yet been reviewed by legal, and the contract's value and exact award date haven't been confirmed.

A supplier on one of our contracts keeps missing the performance targets we set, even after we've raised it with them and given them a chance to sort it out. Can we terminate for that on its own, and separately, do we have any obligation to report or publish anything about the poor performance?
